literal: There was a Daoist named Mituo who could speak barbarian tongues; Emperor Suzong kept him at his side.
idiomatic: A Daoist called Mituo, fluent in the northern languages, served at Emperor Suzong's elbow.

literal: The Empress Dowager feared he would carry messages; on the third day of the third month she had him killed in the great south-city lane.
idiomatic: Fearing he might pass intelligence, the Dowager had him slain in the main south-city street on the third day of the third month.

literal: While rewards were posted to recruit the assassins, in the inner palace she also killed the Directors of the Left and Right Guard, Director of the Palace Secretariat Gu Hui, and Shaoda—all men the emperor favored.
idiomatic: Bounties were still out for the killers when she struck again inside the palace, executing the guard directors, Gu Hui of the Palace Secretariat, and Shaoda, each a favorite of the throne.

literal: Between mother and son, suspicion and rifts arose repeatedly.
idiomatic: Mother and son nursed grievance after grievance.

literal: Zheng Yan, fearing disaster, joined the Empress Dowager in a plot: when Lady Pan the Beautiful bore a daughter, the Dowager falsely announced a son, then proclaimed a general amnesty and changed the reign era.
idiomatic: Dreading ruin, Zheng Yan conspired with the Dowager: when Lady Pan bore a girl, she was passed off as a boy, a great amnesty was declared, and the era name was changed.

literal: Emperor Suzong's death came suddenly; contemporary opinion unanimously blamed the schemes of Zheng Yan and Xu He.
idiomatic: Suzong's end was abrupt; everyone said Zheng Yan and Xu He had engineered it.

literal: Court and countryside alike groaned in anger.
idiomatic: Grief and outrage spread through court and realm.

literal: The Empress Dowager then presented Lady Pan's daughter, saying the crown prince had ascended.
idiomatic: The Dowager then installed Lady Pan's daughter, announcing that the heir had taken the throne.

literal: After several days, seeing hearts had settled, she declared that Lady Pan had in fact borne a daughter and that a successor must now be chosen anew.
idiomatic: When she judged opinion had calmed, she admitted the child was a girl and said a new heir must be chosen.

literal: They then installed Zhao, son of the Prince of Lin Tao, as ruler—he was just three years old—and the realm was stunned.
idiomatic: Zhao, the Lin Tao prince's three-year-old son, was enthroned, and the empire reeled.

literal: Empress Hu, consort of Emperor Xiaoming, was daughter of Sheng, governor of Jizhou and cousin of Empress Ling.
idiomatic: Empress Hu of Emperor Xiaoming was the daughter of Sheng, Jizhou governor and a cousin of Empress Ling.

literal: Empress Ling wished to honor her clan, so she had her made empress.
idiomatic: Empress Ling meant to exalt her house and had her raised to the throne.

literal: Emperor Suzong had a penchant for wine and favored exclusively Lady Pan the Beautiful; the empress and other consorts received no undue favor.
idiomatic: Suzong drank heavily and doted only on Lady Pan; neither the empress nor the other ladies won special favor.

literal: The Empress Dowager selected consorts for Suzong and suppressed those who sought advancement.
idiomatic: The Dowager chose his women herself and crushed anyone who pushed for rank.

literal: At the time the daughters of Cui Xiaofen of Boling, Lu Daoyue of Fanyang, Li Zan of Longxi, and others were made only palace women of lower rank.
idiomatic: Daughters of families such as Cui Xiaofen of Boling, Lu Daoyue of Fanyang, and Li Zan of Longxi were kept merely as palace attendants.

literal: Those who petitioned in lawsuit all met with angry rebuke.
idiomatic: Anyone who sued for better treatment was berated in fury.

literal: At the start of Wutai, after the empress took the tonsure, she resided at Yaoguang Temple.
idiomatic: When Wutai began she entered religion and lived at Yaoguang Temple.

literal: Empress Gao, consort of Emperor Xiaojing, was the second daughter of King Xianwu of Qi.
idiomatic: Empress Gao of Emperor Xiaojing was the second daughter of Qi’s King Xianwu.

literal: In Tianping year 4 an edict betrothed her as empress; the king repeatedly declined, but the emperor would not permit it.
idiomatic: In Tianping year 4 she was summoned as empress; the king refused again and again, but the emperor would not hear of it.

literal: At the start of Xinghe, edicts ordered Chamberlain Sun Teng, Minister of Works Prince of Xiangcheng Xu, concurrently Director of the Department of State Affairs and Governor of Sizhou Prince of Xihe Cong, acting Director of Imperial Sacrifices and Director of Imperial Clansmen Yuan Xiaoyou and others to perform the rites and equip palace officials and guards; the empress was escorted by carriage from the chancellor's mansion at Jinyang.
idiomatic: Early in Xinghe, Sun Teng as chamberlain, Prince Xu of Xiangcheng as minister of works, Prince Cong of Xihe as acting director of the secretariat and Sizhou governor, Yuan Xiaoyou as acting director of sacrifices and director of clansmen, and others were charged to conduct the rites, furnish palace staff and guards, and bring the empress by carriage from the chancellor’s house at Jinyang.

literal: In the fifth month she was installed as empress and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
idiomatic: In the fifth month she was crowned and the realm was pardoned.

literal: When Qi received the abdication she was demoted to Princess of Zhongshan.
idiomatic: After Qi took the mandate she became Princess of Zhongshan.

literal: Later she married down to Yang Zunyan, Left Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
idiomatic: She later wed Yang Zunyan, left vice-director of the secretariat.

literal: The historian says: The founding ancestor was born of a celestial maiden and his line flourished afterward.
idiomatic: The historian writes: The founder sprang from a heaven-sent maiden, and his house prospered for generations.

literal: Empress Ling was licentious and willful; she ultimately lost the realm.
idiomatic: Empress Ling gave way to lust and arrogance and in the end lost the empire.

literal: Is this not where the warning against women who topple states applies?
idiomatic: Was the lesson of cities laid waste not written here?

literal: Gouyi was young when her son was young; Emperor Wu of Han therefore acted expediently, and in Wei times it became regular practice.
idiomatic: Lady Gouyi was still a child when her son was an infant; Han Wudi seized that moment as expedient policy, and under Wei it hardened into custom.

literal: When the son is honored the mother dies—is not the corrective overdone!
idiomatic: Honor the son, kill the mother—has the remedy not swung too far?

literal: Emperor Gaozu finally abolished this abuse; he had good reason.
idiomatic: Gaozu at last swept the abuse away, and rightly so.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: Wei shu juan 13: Various editions' tables of contents mark this juan "deficient." The Baipu, Nan, Ji, and Ju editions all have Song-dynasty collation notes at the end of the juan stating: "The Wei shu biographies of empresses are lost; later persons supplemented them from the Beishi, and also added material from the Gaoshi xiaoshi and the Xiufen dian yulan."
idiomatic: Wei shu juan 13: In several editions the table of contents labels this scroll "lacunose." Baipu, Nan, Ji, and Ju copies alike carry a Song note at the juan’s end: the empress chapters of Wei Shou’s original are missing; later editors patched them from Beishi and padded them with Gaoshi xiaoshi and Xiufen dian yulan.

literal: " The Dian edition places this in Kaozheng and only says: "The Wei shu is lost; later persons supplemented it."
idiomatic: " The Dian edition tucks the matter into Kaozheng and merely says, "Wei Shou’s text is gone; what follows is later supplementation."

idiomatic: Zhao had just succeeded; He Yizhi and Mu Yilu, sons of Wen Shamo Khan, had split the state in three, each holding a third; Zhao’s second regnal year was also He’s second.

idiomatic: Note: "Xian's envoys" means the agents Liu Xian sent to kill Tuoba Gui; "bu shi" (did not have) here is likely a transposition.
